evidence: Cic. Mil. 39: illīus adversāriī, dēfēnsōrēs meī
terms.comment: Rome had no standing opposition: there were opponents of a man or a measure, adversāriī, the commonest classical sense of the word, used of rivals in any contest, elections included (Lewis & Short). A rival candidate is competītor (Traupman 179). None of our sources gives a term for the opposition in a parliament; say who is meant.
Factiō is mostly a word of reproach, a clique (see party, political); partēs adversae is the neutral way to put it.

phrases.latin: septem praetōrēs, octō tribūnī plēbeī, illīus adversāriī, dēfēnsōrēs meī
phrases.english: seven praetors, eight tribunes of the people, his opponents and my defenders
